item.title: Small sheds link China's farms to greener waste management
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
SHENYANG, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- A used pesticide bottle is worth little as recycled material. Collecting, transporting and disposing of it can cost more than it is worth. The economics are difficult right from the start. In Chaoyang, a farming city in northeast China's Liaoning Province, farms and villages are widely dispersed, while used pesticide containers are small, scattered and sometimes still carry chemical residue. Local authorities are testing one option for dealing with this challenge: put collection points as close to the fields as possible. Across the city, 4,228 village collection sheds funnel used pesticide containers into 143 township stations, the first steps in a system designed to keep them out of fields and waterways. "For the first time, bottles, cans, barrels and bags once scattered around the fields have a fixed place to go close to the farmland," said Shang Da, head of the rural development division of the Chaoyang municipal agriculture and rural affairs bureau. Distance matters. Sending county or township vehicles from household to household would be costly and inefficient, while collection points only in township centers could be too far away for farmers to use regularly, Shang explained. By putting the sheds close to the fields, Chaoyang is trying to make proper disposal easier at the point where the waste is generated. Yet building these sheds deals with only one dimension of the waste disposal challenge, namely by providing farmers with somewhere nearby to place the used containers. Once they have done so, there is the need to figure out who will manage them, how often this waste should be collected and where it ultimately ends up. "If a shed lacks rainproof or seepage-control measures, if records are unclear, or if the waste is not transported away promptly once the shed is full, the shed itself could become a new pollution point," said Liu Xuelei, Party chief of Xiawa Village in Chaoyang's Taohuatu Township. National regulations set out responsibilities for how such waste should be collected and handled. Measures issued by the Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs in 2020 assign responsibilities to pesticide producers, sellers and users, require counties, townships and villages to reasonably arrange collection points, and require sellers and collection stations to keep records of volumes and destinations for at least two years. Other regions in China are exploring different approaches to pesticide-packaging collection and disposal. In Yichang, central China's Hubei Province, more than 2,000 collection points have been incorporated into an electronic record system. Local authorities have encouraged 14 agricultural-input firms to form a specialized recycling and treatment company, while incentives including one yuan (about 15 U.S. cents) per 500 grams of returned packaging and redeemable points are used to encourage farmers to participate. Over the past few years, the city's pesticide-packaging recovery rate has reached 82.8 percent, with the waste treated through high-temperature incineration for harmless disposal and energy use. In Jindong District of Jinhua, east China's Zhejiang Province, meanwhile, specially designed collection sheds are being made to keep out rain and prevent leaks and spillage. Records of pesticide purchases are compared with packaging returns, while farmers who have bought more but returned less are reminded to hand in the remaining containers. "Villagers are already used to returning empty pesticide bottles and bags for money," said Ding Jianguo, head of an agricultural-input outlet in Jindong. "It is now uncommon to see them discarded casually in the village." The collection push comes at a time when China is also seeking to reduce its use of agricultural chemicals. Data from the National Bureau of Statistics show that agricultural fertilizer use fell to 49.71 million tonnes in 2025, down 5.3 percent from 2020, while pesticide use in crop production declined to 237,500 tonnes. Zhang Sining, a researcher with the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, said collection systems require public funding to cover start-up and fallback costs, extended responsibility from producers and business operators, and digital records to reduce oversight costs. Administrative mobilization may help collect waste during busy farming seasons but is difficult to sustain year-round, she said, while relying entirely on the market would make it hard to cover remote villages where the waste has little value and transport distances are long. For Chaoyang, the next task is therefore not simply to add more sheds. Xi Haijun, deputy director of the city's agricultural development service center, said the focus will be on adjusting collection frequency according to the farming calendar, keeping records accurately, ensuring the waste has a clear destination, and bringing pesticide producers, sellers and professional treatment companies into a broader cost-sharing mechanism. The sheds may be small but are playing their part in the bigger challenge of keeping bottles and other containers moving from fields to their final destination. ■

item.title: U.S. record 40 trillion-dollar debts fuel global financial risks
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
* The total debt of the U.S. federal government once again hit a historic high, surpassing 40 trillion U.S. dollars on Wednesday. * In the 21st century, the federal debt has been turned into a routine financing tool, launching a debt snowball. * The IMF's latest Global Financial Stability Report warns that rising fragility in the U.S. Treasury market could amplify cross-market risk spillovers. BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- The total debt of the U.S. federal government once again hit a historic high, surpassing 40 trillion U.S. dollars on Wednesday. The latest U.S. Department of the Treasury data showed that the fresh debt record of 40.047 trillion dollars is nearly 10 trillion dollars more than last year's gross domestic product (GDP), or approximately 116,480 dollars in federal debt per American. As the United States is the world's largest sovereign debt market, its unchecked debt growth not only exposes deep structural fiscal problems at home, but also exports risks through the dollar-based financial system, posing a sustained threat to global financial stability and economic recovery. How did U.S. debt soar to this record high? What is the fiscal predicament? And how does this situation push up global financial risks? DEBT SNOWBALL "The scale of U.S. borrowing has expanded exponentially and to a level almost beyond comprehension over two and a half centuries," said a Newsweek online article. The U.S. national debt on the Treasury Department's records started from a modest 71 million dollars in the late 18th century, more than a decade after the nation's independence in 1776. It reached the milestone of 1 trillion dollars in about 200 years, and 10 trillion dollars in the next about 27 years. After that, the U.S. debt swelled to 30 trillion dollars in just 14 years, and to over 40 trillion dollars in the four years since. History reveals an accelerating pace of U.S. debt growth over the past half a century. In the 20th century, national debt became a key tool of federal fiscal policy and a critical instrument for responding to major crises. And in 1981, under the administration of President Ronald Reagan, it crossed the trillion-dollar mark. In the 21st century, the federal debt has been turned into a routine financing tool, launching a debt snowball. In recent years, despite the absence of any major crisis or disruption, the annual U.S. debt increase has kept a pace of more than 2 trillion dollars, twice that of economic expansion. It shows an intensifying snowballing effect, under a fiscal framework yet without automatic brakes to slow this momentum. FISCAL WOES "The greatest threat to our future is hidden in plain sight," warned a recent commentary on Fox News. It pointed out that the swelling federal debt is the biggest hidden danger -- with debt rising year after year, Washington has yet to offer any substantive solutions. The 40 trillion-dollar milestone is not just a number; it marks a significant deterioration in U.S. fiscal sustainability, signaling deepening structural fiscal crises and the continued accumulation of multiple risks. First, persistently high debt leverage has weakened fiscal resilience. As total debt soars, the U.S. government debt-to-GDP ratio remains elevated, reaching 123 percent by the end of the first quarter of 2026, well above the internationally recognized 60 percent warning level. The mounting debt burden continues to crowd out available fiscal resources, leaving the government with increasingly limited fiscal flexibility to support industries, invest in public welfare, and fund infrastructure development. Kenneth Rogoff, a Harvard University professor and former chief economist of the International Monetary Fund (IMF), said in a recent interview with Japan's Asahi Shimbun that surging debt, rising interest rates and political gridlock have eroded the resilience of the U.S. economy, all of which are typical warning signs of a country heading toward a debt crisis. Second, massive interest payments are squeezing public budgets and worsening fiscal imbalances. At current debt levels, annual interest costs have hit record highs, diverting huge amounts of public funds and gradually leaving the U.S. fiscal system focused largely on servicing its own debt. According to Fortune magazine, U.S. interest payments in the first half of fiscal 2026 totaled 529 billion dollars, or over 88 billion dollars per month, equivalent to combined spending on defense and education. This leaves the government far less room to allocate discretionary public spending. Third, prolonged and disorderly debt issuance is eroding market confidence, dimming the traditional "risk-free" aura of U.S. Treasuries. Backed by dollar hegemony, U.S. debt has long been a core global safe-haven asset. But endless borrowing has raised doubts among global investors about its long-term creditworthiness. Sovereign institutions around the world have continued to adjust their foreign exchange reserve allocations, reducing their holdings of U.S. Treasuries while increasing allocations to gold and other diversified assets. As a result, the global safe-haven premium of U.S. Treasuries has continued to narrow, significantly increasing market vulnerability. Data from the European Central Bank show that by the end of 2025, the share of U.S. Treasuries in global official reserve assets had fallen for two consecutive years, dropping 4 percentage points from the end of 2023. GLOBAL COST As the anchor for global financial pricing and a key barometer of cross-border capital flows, the 40 trillion U.S. debt burden could transmit risks globally through channels including higher financing costs, disruptions to cross-border capital movements and reduced market liquidity, triggering prolonged and widespread negative spillover effects. Massive U.S. debt supply raises global risk-free rates, stifling the recovery. With Washington continuing to borrow heavily to cover fiscal deficits, growing concerns over the sustainability of its massive debt burden are pushing up risk premiums and driving long-term U.S. Treasury yields steadily higher. As the benchmark for global asset pricing, higher U.S. Treasury yields drive up borrowing costs for sovereign bonds, corporate dollar debt, and consumer credit worldwide. Emerging markets face heavier foreign-currency debt burdens, while global corporate investment and financing costs rise, dampening industrial expansion, cross-border investment and consumer credit demand. Rising long-term yields create a "suction effect" for dollar assets, intensifying global capital and currency volatility. High-yield U.S. Treasuries continue to attract global funds back to the United States, causing large-scale capital outflows from emerging market equity and bond markets. Data from Reuters and Bloomberg show that, as U.S. debt approaches the 40 trillion-dollar mark, long-term Treasury yields have fluctuated upward, prompting large-scale and frequent shifts in cross-border capital flows and further widening the divergence between financial markets in developed economies and emerging markets. Disorderly debt expansion also distorts bond market structures, weakens liquidity, and heightens global systemic risks. The U.S. Treasury market, once a cornerstone of global financial stability, is now experiencing supply-demand imbalances. Its ownership structure has fundamentally shifted: long-term allocators like foreign central banks and sovereign wealth funds are consistently reducing their holdings, while short-term leveraged players such as hedge funds are stepping in as major buyers. As a result, U.S. Treasuries, long regarded as a global stabilizer, are increasingly becoming a source of market volatility. Any shift in economic data, monetary policy or geopolitical conditions could trigger concentrated selling, leading to sharp moves in yields and sudden liquidity freezes. The IMF's latest Global Financial Stability Report warns that rising fragility in the U.S. Treasury market could amplify cross-market risk spillovers, turning localized financial shocks into global disruptions and steadily weakening the self-correcting capacity of the international financial system. International observers broadly agree that the 40 trillion-dollar U.S. debt burden is not merely a fiscal issue for the United States alone; it has become a source of global systemic risks. The United States is using the dollar's dominant position to externalize the costs of its fiscal imbalances, not only weighing on the global economic recovery but also continuing to undermine the existing international financial order. Over the long term, vulnerabilities in the global financial system and underlying structural imbalances will only continue to accumulate. ■

item.title: China adds Kyrgyzstan, Vietnam to 240-hour visa-free transit program
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- China has added Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam to its 240-hour visa-free transit program, bringing the total number of countries eligible for this policy to 57, immigration authorities announced on Thursday. Effective from Aug. 20, citizens of Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam holding ordinary passports and interline passenger tickets with confirmed dates and itineraries bound for a third country or region may enter China through any of the 65 ports across the country and stay up to 240 hours, or 10 days, without a visa, according to the National Immigration Administration (NIA). Citizens of these two countries who hold ordinary passports will also be eligible for the 30-day visa-free entry policy for Hainan Province in south China starting the same day. This will allow them to enter the province through Hainan's open ports and stay visa-free for up to 30 days. With these additions, the number of countries covered by this Hainan visa-free policy has now reached 61. During the visa-free period, travelers are permitted to engage in tourism, business, exchange visits and family visits. However, the two policies do not cover employment, study or journalistic activities, which still require appropriate visas, the NIA said. These measures are part of China's broader efforts to boost international travel and exchanges following the COVID-19 pandemic. In December 2024, authorities extended the visa-free transit window from 72 or 144 hours to 240 hours. The country has also expanded its unilateral visa-free access program, allowing travelers from 50 countries to stay for up to 30 days. These sweeping policy changes have facilitated increased travel to China, fueling a surge in online content and interest in "China Travel," particularly on platforms like YouTube. China's border authorities handled a record 369 million inbound and outbound crossings in the first half of 2026, up 10.8 percent year-on-year, according to the NIA. Foreign arrivals in China rose, with visa-free entries surging 30.6 percent year on year to exceed 17.8 million during the same period, accounting for more than three-quarters of all foreign arrivals. Vietnam was China's fourth largest source of inbound travelers in the first half of this year, after the Republic of Korea, Russia, and Malaysia, according to the NIA data. Chinese regions bordering Vietnam have been popular destinations among Vietnamese travelers. Hekou Port in southwest China's Yunnan Province, for example, recorded more than 4 million border crossings between China and Vietnam from the beginning of this year until Aug. 13, up 5.24 percent year on year, including travelers in more than 20,000 tourist groups. Nguyen Duc Kha, who works for a fruit exporter in Vietnam, believes that the new visa-free transit policy will offer more convenience for frequent cross-border business travelers and encourage more Vietnamese visitors to explore a wider range of destinations in China. "At present, Hainan is not yet a very popular destination among Vietnamese tourists," Kha noted. "I hope this visa policy, together with Hainan's expansion of entertainment and recreational services, will attract more Vietnamese visitors." Meanwhile, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, which borders Kyrgyzstan and several other Asian countries, recorded more than 2.4 million border-crossing trips in the first half of this year, a 33.2 percent rise from the same period last year. Its Torugart Port connecting China and Kyrgyzstan recorded more than 64,000 inbound and outbound trips in the first quarter, a year-on-year increase of 60 percent. ■

item.title: Robot conference spotlights commercial push for China's robot sector
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- At an exhibition hall, about 10 humanoid robots worked in a coordinated workflow, with some lifting and stacking boxes and others sorting goods along an assembly line. Together, they demonstrated a complete smart logistics process -- from material handling to sorting and replenishment. This scene, presented by humanoid robot maker UBTECH at the 2026 World Robot Conference (WRC) in Beijing, conveys one message: robots are quickly evolving from showpieces to real-world applications. The conference, which runs from Wednesday through Sunday, has drawn more than 300 exhibitors from 26 countries, with over 3,000 products on display, including more than 300 debuts. At the Galaxea display area, visitors scanned a QR code to order a bottle of water. A robot autonomously navigated through the warehouse to fetch and package the water in just over one minute, relying solely on model-based recognition. This system is already up and running in Beijing and other cities. "The solution can solve overnight warehouse staffing problems," said Luo Tianqi, chief financial officer of Galaxea. "Nighttime order volumes aren't huge, but still require people on night shifts. Replacing them with robots is economically viable." China's humanoid robot industry is entering a critical stage of large-scale commercialization and deployment, as embodied intelligence products move from small-batch trials to broader adoption, Xu Xiaolan, chairwoman of the Chinese Institute of Electronics, said at the 2026 WRC. Nearly 10 major automakers, including BYD and SAIC, are already testing embodied-intelligence systems on production lines for tasks like material handling and parts loading. Embodied-intelligence robots are also operating in high-risk, confined spaces for disaster relief, flood response and hazardous industrial inspections, Xu added. Unitree Robotics founder and CEO Wang Xingxing said at the conference that the company's robots are already being tested on auto assembly lines and in its own factories, with AI research focused on improving their ability to perform practical tasks in homes and industrial environments. On Wednesday, the Hangzhou-based company became the first humanoid robot maker listed on the A-share market, marking a significant step for the country's humanoid robot industry. This year's conference has also emphasized industrial chain collaboration. The WRC brings together AI algorithm developers, 3D-vision and battery suppliers, robot makers and end-users to facilitate cooperation and shorten R&D and iteration cycles. According to the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, revenue for China's robotics sector exceeded 300 billion yuan (about 44.24 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, with average annual growth of over 20 percent in the past five years. In the first half of 2026, revenue reached 165.5 billion yuan, up 24.5 percent year on year. Chinese robots have demonstrated their technological prowess through impressive feats, ranging from martial arts to marathons. Meanwhile, China is doubling down on expanding robots' real-world applications, despite predictions that the industry's "GPT moment" remains years away. Across the country, China has already built more than 70 embodied-intelligence training grounds as of June, with 46 more under construction or being planned, according to a report by the China Academy of Information and Communications Technology. The industry has benefited from supportive national strategy. "Embodied intelligence" was first written into China's government work report in 2025. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for a forward-looking layout of future industries, including embodied artificial intelligence, as well as mechanisms to boost funding and share risks in these emerging sectors. Wang said "a ChatGPT moment in embodied intelligence" will come when robots can be dropped into unfamiliar settings and complete most tasks via simple voice or text commands. He expects that such a breakthrough could occur within two to three years in an optimistic scenario, or within five to ten years at the latest. ■

item.title: China urges U.S. to immediately repeal Section 232 tariffs on drones, parts
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Commerce on Thursday urged the United States to immediately repeal its Section 232 tariff measures on drones and drone parts, saying the measures severely harm the interests of Chinese enterprises and disrupt cooperation in global drone industrial and supply chains. China has consistently maintained that the U.S. Section 232 measures constitute unilateralism and protectionism carried out under the pretext of "national security," said commerce ministry spokesperson He Yadong at a regular media conference in response to a question concerning the U.S. decision to impose the tariffs. In fact, Chinese drones exported to the United States are mainly used in civilian applications, including agriculture, equipment inspection, and film and television entertainment, He said. He said the U.S. Section 232 measures overstretch the concept of national security, impose differentiated tariff rates on trading partners, and discriminate against relevant Chinese products. The measures further undermine a market environment featuring fair competition, the spokesperson said. "China firmly opposes this." At the media conference, the spokesperson also responded to the U.S. allegation of a "shadow transshipment network," calling it a false narrative and fabrication. He said that the U.S. report entitled "The Great Transshipment Scam: Rise, Scope, and Costs" disregards the facts and distorts right and wrong by denouncing normal international trade and investment as a "scam." This is a typical act of unilateralism and protectionism aimed at suppressing and blocking Chinese products, the spokesperson said. "China is strongly dissatisfied with and firmly opposed to this." He said that, in fact, it is the United States' excessively high and differentiated tariffs that are the fundamental cause of the threats to the security of global supply chains. By attributing its domestic economic problems to external factors, the United States will not be able to resolve its own deep-seated problems, He said. China urges the United States to immediately stop its irresponsible accusations, stop undermining China-U.S. economic and trade relations, and genuinely safeguard the security and stability of global industrial and supply chains, the spokesperson said. He said China has always complied with international economic and trade rules and will continue to conduct economic and trade cooperation with all parties on the basis of equality and mutual benefit, jointly build a trade network of mutual benefit and win-win outcomes, and make positive contributions to global development and prosperity. ■

item.title: China reshapes housing provident fund management rules as property market enters new phase
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- China on Tuesday announced a decision to revise its regulations regarding housing provident fund management, in the latest effort to adapt the long-standing housing finance system to a property market entering a new development phase. The revised regulations, set to take effect on Sept. 20, will expand the scope for withdrawals, improve the efficiency of fund management and related services, strengthen risk prevention, and extend coverage to a broader range of workers, among other measures. The revision marks a significant update to the housing provident fund system, which has been in place for more than two decades and covers about 180 million workers. Experts said the move is expected to help unlock housing demand and support a more stable property market over the longer term. China's housing provident fund is a policy-based housing finance system funded by mandatory monthly contributions from employers and employees. Established during the country's rapid urbanization in the 1990s, the system has helped millions of urban workers secure homes and played an important role in easing housing shortages. However, a system designed primarily around home purchases has become less suited to an ever-evolving market. Meanwhile, withdrawal restrictions have left substantial savings parked in individual accounts for long periods. Data from the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development showed that housing provident fund balances stood at roughly 10.93 trillion yuan (about 1.62 trillion U.S. dollars) at the end of 2024, underscoring the potential to further revitalize dormant liquidity within the system. To better meet diverse housing needs and put more of the funds to use, the revised rules expand the qualifying withdrawal categories from six to nine. New additions include renovations of owner-occupied homes, property management fees and other housing-related spending approved by the State Council. This reform also seeks to adapt the system to China's changing labor market. Self-employed individuals, part-time workers and others in flexible employment will be allowed to make voluntary contributions and receive policy support under the revised regulations, potentially opening the door for more than 200 million flexible workers to participate in the system. Contribution records will also be mutually recognized nationwide, making it easier to transfer provident fund accounts and apply for loans across urban areas. Chen Wenjing, director of policy research at the China Index Academy, said the change could provide long-term support to the development of city clusters and metropolitan areas, as well as the freer flow of labor and other production factors. The revision is part of a broader shift in China's housing policy, as the market moves away from an emphasis on new construction toward upgrading existing homes. The Central Economic Work Conference in December last year called for deeper reform of the housing provident fund system, a direction also reflected in the country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). Local governments have already moved to expand the ways in which residents can tap their housing provident fund savings. In the first seven months of 2026, more than 60 cities adjusted their housing provident fund policies, rolling out measures including higher loan limits, lower down-payment requirements, broader withdrawal rules, expanded coverage and new services. In Huaibei, east China's Anhui Province, provident fund savings can now be withdrawn for age- and child-friendly home renovations, while in Zhuhai, south China's Guangdong Province, employees can now use their provident fund savings to help renovate homes owned by their spouses, parents or children. Li Yujia, chief researcher at the Guangdong Housing Policy Research Center, said the changes are part of a broader effort to make the housing provident fund more responsive to people's diverse housing needs. The revision would accelerate the fund's transition from a financing tool centered on home purchases to a comprehensive support across the entire housing lifecycle, from buying and renting to renovating and maintaining homes, Li explained. ■

item.title: China to support 3 mln industrial workers in further education, skills upgrading
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- China will provide financial support for at least 3 million industrial workers in pursuing further education and upgrading skills by 2030, according to a plan released Thursday by the All-China Federation of Trade Unions. The plan, covering the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), outlines measures to improve the skills development system for industrial workers and promote their all-round development. It also sets targets for cultivating skilled talent. By 2030, China aims to foster around 1,000 national-level master artisans, 5,000 provincial-level master artisans and 25,000 city-level master artisans. The total number of innovation studios for model workers and master artisans is expected to reach 160,000 by 2030, the plan said. The initiative comes as China steps up efforts to upgrade its industrial sector. The country's 15th Five-Year Plan places building a modern industrial system high on the agenda. China also set a dual strategy focusing on investment in "both physical assets and human capital" to advance innovation-driven, demand-led growth, with vocational skills training identified as one of the key areas to equip the workforce. Thursday's plan calls for improving the lifelong vocational skills training system and helping workers adapt their skills to changing needs. "AI Plus" learning and training programs will be carried out, alongside the development of a national skills learning platform for industrial workers. Training services will also be strengthened for migrant workers, workers in new forms of employment and young workers, while a system of craftsman colleges combining online and offline learning will be developed. Wang Xiaoping, minister of human resources and social security, said earlier that China will deepen large-scale vocational skills training this year. Targeted training will focus on sectors such as the low-altitude economy, new energy vehicles, AI, and elderly care services, in a bid to better align skills development with industrial and employment needs. ■

item.title: China honors Shenzhou-21 mission astronauts with medals
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- Three astronauts from the Shenzhou-21 crewed mission were awarded medals for their service to China's space endeavors on Thursday. Zhang Lu was honored with a second-class aerospace achievement medal, while Wu Fei and Zhang Hongzhang received third-class medals and the honorary title of "heroic astronauts." The awards were given by the Communist Party of China Central Committee, the State Council, and the Central Military Commission. Zhang Lu, the mission commander and a veteran astronaut on his second spaceflight, holds the record for the most spacewalks by a Chinese astronaut. Wu, the spaceflight engineer of the crew, is the youngest Chinese astronaut so far to carry out extravehicular activities. Zhang Hongzhang, the payload specialist of the crew, oversaw a slew of scientific experiments in the space station, including the projects he co-designed. The Shenzhou-21 crew spent 210 days in orbit, from their launch on Oct. 31, 2025 to their return on May 29, 2026, setting a new record for the longest single crew stay by Chinese astronauts. ■

item.title: Xi congratulates Hichilema on re-election as Zambian president
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-20
BEIJING, Aug. 20 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday congratulated Hakainde Hichilema on his re-election as president of Zambia. In his message, Xi said that they have met twice in recent years, and jointly steered the development of China-Zambia relations. The political mutual trust between the two countries has continued to deepen, practical cooperation has been fruitful, and China and Zambia have closely coordinated and cooperated in multilateral affairs, he said. Xi said he attaches great importance to the development of China-Zambia ties, and stands ready to work with Hichilema to implement the outcomes of the Beijing Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation. He also pledged to join the Zambian leader in carrying forward traditional friendship, cementing mutual support, and continuously raising the level of mutually beneficial cooperation, so as to take the China-Zambia comprehensive strategic cooperative partnership to new heights and deliver greater benefits to the two peoples. ■
